topics.title: Ratios, Rates, Percentages & Rational Numbers
topics.summary: Connecting ratios, unit rates, fractions, decimals, and percentages in real-world problem solving.
keyFormulas: Unit Rate = Quantity A / Quantity B
sourceNotes: A ratio compares two quantities multiplicatively (e.g., 3:5); a rate compares quantities with different units (e.g., km/h).
Percent literally means 'per hundred' (out of 100). To convert a fraction to a percentage, multiply by 100%.
Dividing by a fraction is equivalent to multiplying by its reciprocal: (a/b) ÷ (c/d) = (a/b) × (d/c).
topics.workedExample: A train travels 240 km in 3 hours. Its unit rate (average speed) is 240 ÷ 3 = 80 km/h. In 5 hours at the same rate, it travels 80 × 5 = 400 km.
topics.commonMisconception: Treating a part-to-part ratio of 2:3 as the fraction 2/3 of the whole (the fraction of the whole is actually 2/(2+3) = 2/5 = 40%).
learningObjectives: Connecting ratios, unit rates, fractions, decimals, and percentages in real-world problem solving.

topics.title: Introduction to Algebraic Expressions & One-Step Equations
topics.summary: Variables, coefficients, combining like terms, distributive property, and solving x + a = b and ax = b.
keyFormulas: Distributive Law: a(b + c) = ab + ac
Inverse Operations: if x + a = b then x = b - a
sourceNotes: A variable is a symbol (such as x or n) representing an unknown or changing numerical value; a coefficient is the number multiplying the variable.
Only 'like terms' (terms with the exact same variable and exponent) can be combined by adding or subtracting their coefficients.
topics.workedExample: Simplify 3(2x + 4) + 5x: First distribute 3 -> 6x + 12 + 5x. Then combine like terms 6x + 5x -> 11x + 12.
topics.commonMisconception: Distributing only to the first term inside parentheses: writing 3(2x + 4) = 6x + 4 instead of 6x + 12.
learningObjectives: Variables, coefficients, combining like terms, distributive property, and solving x + a = b and ax = b.

topics.title: SI Units, Mass, Volume & Density
topics.summary: Measuring physical quantities using SI units, water displacement for irregular solids, and density calculations.
sourceNotes: Density is mass per unit volume (g/cm³ or kg/m³). An object floats in a fluid if its average density is less than the fluid's density.
To find the volume of an irregular stone, submerge it in a measuring cylinder and compute V_final - V_initial (Archimedes displacement).
topics.workedExample: A metal block has mass 270 g and dimensions 10 cm × 5 cm × 2 cm (V = 100 cm³). Density ρ = 270 g / 100 cm³ = 2.7 g/cm³ (Aluminum).
topics.commonMisconception: Thinking a larger piece of iron has a greater density than a small iron nail (both have the exact same density of ~7.87 g/cm³).
learningObjectives: Measuring physical quantities using SI units, water displacement for irregular solids, and density calculations.

topics.title: Cell Structure: Plant vs. Animal Cells
topics.summary: Organelles (nucleus, cell membrane, cytoplasm, mitochondria, chloroplasts, cell wall, vacuole) and microscopy.
keyFormulas: Total Magnification = Eyepiece Lens × Objective Lens
Plant-Only: Cell Wall, Chloroplasts, Large Central Vacuole
sourceNotes: All living organisms are composed of cells. The nucleus contains DNA and controls cell activities; mitochondria release energy via cellular respiration.
Plant cells have a rigid cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts for photosynthesis, and a permanent large central vacuole, which animal cells lack.
topics.workedExample: Using a 10× eyepiece and a 40× objective lens on an onion epidermis slide gives a total magnification of 10 × 40 = 400×.
topics.commonMisconception: Assuming plant cells only perform photosynthesis and do not have mitochondria for cellular respiration.
learningObjectives: Organelles (nucleus, cell membrane, cytoplasm, mitochondria, chloroplasts, cell wall, vacuole) and microscopy.

topics.title: Plot Architecture & Figurative Language
topics.summary: Exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution; simile, metaphor, personification, and hyperbole.
keyFormulas: Plot Arc: Exposition -> Rising Action -> Climax -> Falling Action -> Resolution
sourceNotes: Similes compare two distinct things using 'like' or 'as'; metaphors state that one thing IS another to transfer meaning directly.
The climax is the turning point of maximum tension where the protagonist confronts the central conflict.
topics.workedExample: 'The classroom was a zoo' is a metaphor implying chaotic noise; 'He ran like the wind' is a simile emphasizing speed.
topics.commonMisconception: Identifying the climax as the very end of the story rather than the decisive turning point.
learningObjectives: Exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution; simile, metaphor, personification, and hyperbole.

topics.title: Integers, Signed Rational Numbers & Two-Step Equations
topics.summary: Adding, subtracting, multiplying, and dividing positive/negative integers and solving ax + b = c.
sourceNotes: Subtracting a number is identical to adding its additive inverse (opposite): a - b = a + (-b).
To solve a two-step linear equation ax + b = c, undo addition/subtraction first (ax = c - b), then undo multiplication/division (x = (c - b)/a).
topics.workedExample: Solve -3x + 7 = 22: Subtract 7 from both sides -> -3x = 15. Divide both sides by -3 -> x = -5.
topics.commonMisconception: Forgetting to flip the sign when dividing by a negative coefficient (writing x = 5 instead of x = -5).
learningObjectives: Adding, subtracting, multiplying, and dividing positive/negative integers and solving ax + b = c.

topics.title: Circles (Circumference & Area), Proportions & Probability
topics.summary: Pi (π), circumference C = 2πr, area A = πr², proportional relationships y = kx, and sample spaces.
keyFormulas: Probability: P(E) = Favorable Outcomes / Total Outcomes
sourceNotes: Pi (π ≈ 3.14159 or 22/7) is the constant ratio of any circle's circumference to its diameter.
Notice that radius is half the diameter (r = d/2). Always convert diameter to radius before applying A = πr².
topics.workedExample: A circular track has diameter 14 m (so radius r = 7 m). Using π ≈ 22/7, Area = (22/7) × 7² = 22 × 7 = 154 m².
topics.commonMisconception: Plugging the diameter directly into A = πr² without halving it first, or confusing 2πr with πr².
learningObjectives: Pi (π), circumference C = 2πr, area A = πr², proportional relationships y = kx, and sample spaces.

topics.title: Speed, Motion & Distance-Time Graphs
topics.summary: Calculating average speed, interpreting slope on distance-time graphs, and relative motion.
sourceNotes: On a distance-time graph, a straight diagonal line indicates constant speed; a horizontal flat line indicates the object is stationary (speed = 0).
A steeper gradient on a distance-time graph represents a higher speed.
topics.workedExample: A cyclist covers 150 meters in 10 seconds, rests for 5 seconds, then rides 90 meters in 5 seconds. Average speed = Total Distance / Total Time = 240 m / 20 s = 12 m/s.
topics.commonMisconception: Averaging the two speeds directly instead of dividing total distance by total time (including rest time).
learningObjectives: Calculating average speed, interpreting slope on distance-time graphs, and relative motion.

topics.title: Atoms, Elements, Compounds & Mixtures
topics.summary: Periodic table basics, chemical symbols, covalent/ionic bonding intro, and separation techniques.
keyFormulas: Element = 1 type of atom (e.g., O₂, Fe)
Compound = Chemically bonded elements (e.g., H₂O, NaCl)
sourceNotes: Elements consist of only one kind of atom and cannot be broken down chemically. Compounds have fixed ratios of chemically bonded atoms with properties completely different from their constituent elements.
Mixtures can be separated by physical methods: filtration, evaporation, distillation, or chromatography.
topics.workedExample: Sodium (explosive metal) + Chlorine (toxic green gas) chemically react to form Sodium Chloride (edible table salt, NaCl).
topics.commonMisconception: Thinking air is a pure compound rather than a physical mixture of nitrogen, oxygen, argon, and carbon dioxide.
learningObjectives: Periodic table basics, chemical symbols, covalent/ionic bonding intro, and separation techniques.

topics.title: Ancient Civilizations, The Silk Road & Scientific Golden Ages
topics.summary: Trade networks across Eurasia, cultural/scientific exchange, algebra's origins, and cartography.
keyFormulas: Silk Road: Chang'an -> Samarkand -> Baghdad -> Mediterranean
sourceNotes: The Silk Road was an interconnected network of overland and maritime trade routes linking East Asia, Central Asia, South Asia, the Middle East, and Europe.
Alongside silk, spices, and paper, scholars exchanged mathematics (algebra, Hindu-Arabic numerals), astronomy, and medicine.
topics.workedExample: Paper-making technology traveled from China to Samarkand and Baghdad, enabling libraries like the House of Wisdom to preserve and expand classical and scientific texts.
topics.commonMisconception: Picturing the Silk Road as a single paved highway rather than a shifting web of oasis and sea routes.
learningObjectives: Trade networks across Eurasia, cultural/scientific exchange, algebra's origins, and cartography.

topics.title: Rhetorical Devices, Tone, Mood & Literary Analysis
topics.summary: Deconstructing author's purpose, ethos/pathos/logos, distinguishing tone from mood, and writing textual analysis essays.
learningObjectives: Analyze how an author develops and contrasts the points of view of different characters or narrators
Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative and connotative meanings
keyFormulas: Tone = Author's attitude toward the subject (critical, playful, solemn)
Mood = Emotional atmosphere created for the reader (eerie, joyful, tense)
PEEL Paragraph = Point + Evidence + Explanation + Link to Thesis
sourceNotes: Diction choices directly cultivate tone: choosing 'slender' conveys elegance while 'scrawny' conveys frail awkwardness.
Ethos appeals to authority and ethics, Pathos appeals to audience empathy, Logos appeals to logical data and reasoning.
When analyzing poetry or prose, do not just quote lines—explicitly unpack the connotations of individual keywords.
topics.workedExample: Excerpt: 'The withered branches clawed at the blackened sky.' Tone: Grim, foreboding. Mood: Anxious, apprehensive. Analysis: The verb 'clawed' personifies the trees as predatory beasts.
topics.commonMisconception: Treating tone and mood as identical; tone is the author's voice, mood is the reader's feeling.

topics.title: Linear Equations, Gradient-Intercept (y = mx + c) & Laws of Indices
topics.summary: Solving multi-step linear equations with variables on both sides, graphing lines, and exponent rules.
sourceNotes: In y = mx + c, m is the gradient (rate of change / rise over run) and c is the y-intercept where the line crosses the vertical axis (x = 0).
For indices with the same base: multiply -> add exponents; divide -> subtract exponents; any non-zero base to power 0 equals 1 (a⁰ = 1).
topics.workedExample: Find the equation of the line passing through (0, 3) and (4, 11): Gradient m = (11 - 3)/(4 - 0) = 8/4 = 2. Since y-intercept c = 3, the equation is y = 2x + 3.
topics.commonMisconception: Computing gradient as (x₂ - x₁)/(y₂ - y₁) (run over rise instead of rise over run) or thinking x⁰ = 0.
learningObjectives: Solving multi-step linear equations with variables on both sides, graphing lines, and exponent rules.

topics.title: Pythagoras' Theorem & Algebraic Common Factorisation
topics.summary: Right-angled triangles (a² + b² = c²) and extracting highest common factors (HCF) from algebraic expressions.
keyFormulas: HCF Factorisation: ab + ac = a(b + c)
sourceNotes: In any right-angled triangle, the square of the hypotenuse (longest side opposite the 90° angle) equals the sum of squares of the other two legs.
To factorise an expression completely, extract both the greatest numerical factor and the lowest power of every shared variable.
topics.workedExample: Factorise 12x³y - 18x²y²: The HCF of 12 and 18 is 6; shared variables are x² and y. Factoring out 6x²y leaves 6x²y(2x - 3y).
topics.commonMisconception: Partial factorisation: factoring out 2xy instead of the full HCF 6x²y.
learningObjectives: Right-angled triangles (a² + b² = c²) and extracting highest common factors (HCF) from algebraic expressions.

topics.title: Pressure in Solids/Fluids, Light Refraction & Chemical Reactions
topics.summary: Pressure P = F/A, Snell's qualitative refraction, pH scale, neutralization, and conservation of atoms.
sourceNotes: Pressure is force divided by contact area (P = F/A). A sharp knife cuts easily because a tiny area produces huge pressure from a modest force.
When light travels from air into glass or water (a denser medium), it slows down and bends toward the normal.
Acids have pH < 7 (donate H⁺ ions); alkalis have pH > 7 (donate OH⁻ ions); neutral solutions have pH = 7.
topics.workedExample: A 600 N crate rests on a base of area 0.2 m². Pressure exerted on the floor = 600 N / 0.2 m² = 3,000 Pa (3 kPa).
topics.commonMisconception: Measuring angles of incidence and refraction from the glass surface instead of from the 90° normal line.
learningObjectives: Pressure P = F/A, Snell's qualitative refraction, pH scale, neutralization, and conservation of atoms.

topics.title: Binary Representation, Boolean Logic & Python Functions
topics.summary: Converting binary to denary (base 2 to base 10), AND/OR/NOT gates, lists, and modular functions.
keyFormulas: De Morgan: NOT(A AND B) = (NOT A) OR (NOT B)
sourceNotes: Computers store all data as binary bits (0 and 1). Each bit position represents a power of 2 (2⁰, 2¹, 2² ... 2⁷).
Functions encapsulate reusable logic with parameters and return values, improving readability and modularity.
topics.commonMisconception: Forgetting that array/list indexing in Python starts at index 0 rather than index 1.
learningObjectives: Converting binary to denary (base 2 to base 10), AND/OR/NOT gates, lists, and modular functions.

topics.title: Persuasive Argumentation, Fallacies & Media Literacy
topics.summary: Evaluating argument validity, detecting logical fallacies (ad hominem, straw man, false dilemma), and synthesis writing.
learningObjectives: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is sound and the evidence is relevant and sufficient
Identify when irrelevant evidence is introduced and recognize common logical fallacies
keyFormulas: Valid Argument = Premise 1 + Premise 2 -> Necessary Conclusion
sourceNotes: A sound argument requires both true premises and a logically valid connection to the conclusion.
Logical fallacies undermine credibility: an ad hominem attacks the person rather than addressing their evidence.
In persuasive speechwriting, acknowledge the opposing viewpoint (counterclaim) and refute it with empirical facts.
topics.workedExample: Opposing claim: 'Renewable energy is too expensive to install.' Rebuttal: While upfront capital costs exist, levelized lifecycle costs and environmental savings make renewables cheaper over a 10-year horizon.
topics.commonMisconception: Believing that simply stating your opinion loudly without counterargument refutation makes an argument persuasive.
